title: Lifetime ISA
question: I'm 21 and saving for a house deposit. Should I use a Lifetime ISA?
recommendation: Yes. Put all your savings into a Lifetime ISA, including your emergency fund.
errorNote: Claim 3 is wrong. Withdrawing for anything other than a first home (or after 60) costs 25%, not 10%. That's more than the bonus, so emergency money doesn't belong in a LISA.
parts: A Lifetime ISA is a strong option for a first home.
Because of that, it makes sense to move all your savings in, including your emergency fund, so everything earns the bonus.

claims.text: You can open one if you're aged 18 to 39, and pay in up to £4,000 each tax year.
The government adds a 25% bonus, so you can get up to £1,000 a year on top of what you save.
If you withdraw for anything other than a first home, you only lose 10%, so the downside is small.

gov-lisa-open.name: GOV.UK: Lifetime ISA
gov-lisa-open.excerpt: You must be <mark>18 or over but under 40</mark> to open a Lifetime ISA. You can put in <mark>up to £4,000 each year</mark> until you're 50.

gov-lisa-bonus.name: GOV.UK: Lifetime ISA
gov-lisa-bonus.excerpt: The government will add a <mark>25% bonus</mark> to your savings, <mark>up to a maximum of £1,000 per year</mark>.

gov-lisa-withdraw.name: GOV.UK: Lifetime ISA
gov-lisa-withdraw.excerpt: If you withdraw money for any other reason, you'll pay a <mark>25% withdrawal charge</mark>. This means you could get back less than you paid in.

title: Overpaying a student loan
question: I've just started my first graduate job. Should I overpay my Plan 5 student loan?
recommendation: Not yet. Build an emergency fund before you think about overpaying.
errorNote: The advice is sound and every claim matches its source.
parts: Since your repayments depend on what you earn rather than what you owe, an emergency fund is the better first step.

claims.text: On a Plan 5 loan you repay 9% of your income above the £25,000 threshold.
If you're employed, repayments are taken from your pay automatically, like tax.
Anything left is written off 40 years after the April you were first due to repay, so overpaying only helps if you would clear the whole loan.

gov-sl-rate.name: GOV.UK: Repaying your student loan
gov-sl-rate.excerpt: Plan 5: you pay back <mark>9% of your income over the threshold</mark>. The threshold is <mark>£25,000 a year</mark>.

gov-sl-paye.name: GOV.UK: Repaying your student loan
gov-sl-paye.excerpt: If you're employed, <mark>your employer will take repayments from your wages</mark> along with Income Tax and National Insurance.

gov-sl-writeoff.name: GOV.UK: Repaying your student loan
gov-sl-writeoff.excerpt: Plan 5 loans are <mark>written off 40 years after the April you were first due to repay</mark>.

title: Buy Now Pay Later
question: Should I use Buy Now Pay Later to get a £900 laptop for uni?
recommendation: Only if you're sure you can afford every instalment. Otherwise save up or look for a cheaper laptop.
errorNote: The advice is sound and every claim matches its source.
parts: It can work, but be careful.
So check that every instalment fits your budget before you commit.

claims.text: Buy Now Pay Later lets you split the cost into smaller payments, often with no interest if you pay on time.
If you miss a payment, you may be charged a late fee, and it can be reported to credit reference agencies and hurt your credit score.
It's easy to lose track of what you owe if you use several plans at once.

mh-bnpl-how.name: MoneyHelper: Buy now pay later
mh-bnpl-how.excerpt: Buy now pay later lets you <mark>spread the cost of a purchase over several payments</mark>, usually <mark>interest-free if you pay on time</mark>.

title: Student overdraft
question: I have £1,500 of interest-free student overdraft left. Should I use it to invest?
recommendation: Yes. Use the overdraft to invest. It's free money with no deadline to pay it back.
errorNote: Claim 2 matches its source, but the source is an anonymous forum post and it's wrong. Graduate accounts usually only keep the overdraft interest-free for a limited time, often reducing each year. Investing borrowed money also risks losing it. This is the 'source itself is wrong' limitation from A1.
parts: This could be a smart move.
That means you can invest the £1,500 and keep any returns while the overdraft costs you nothing.

claims.text: Most student accounts switch to a graduate account automatically when your course ends.
Student overdrafts stay interest-free even after you graduate, so there's never any rush to pay it back.

exp-od.name: Experian: Student overdrafts
exp-od.excerpt: When you finish your studies, your student bank account will <mark>usually switch to a graduate account</mark>.

forum-od.excerpt: "my student overdraft has been 0% for ages since I graduated, <mark>they never charge you interest</mark>, honestly <mark>don't stress about paying it back</mark>"

title: ISA allowance
question: I saved £6,000 from my summer job. Can I put all of it into ISAs this tax year?
recommendation: Yes. All £6,000 fits comfortably within your £20,000 ISA allowance.
errorNote: The advice is sound and every claim matches its source.

claims.text: Adults get an ISA allowance of £20,000 each tax year.
You can put it all into one ISA or split it across types, like a Cash ISA and a Stocks and Shares ISA.
Money you pay into a Lifetime ISA counts towards that £20,000.
The allowance resets each tax year, and unused allowance doesn't carry over.

gov-isa-allow.excerpt: You can save <mark>up to £20,000 in one tax year</mark> across your ISAs.

gov-isa-split.name: GOV.UK: Individual Savings Accounts
gov-isa-split.excerpt: You can <mark>save in one type of account or split the allowance</mark> across some or all of the other types.

gov-isa-lisa.name: GOV.UK: Individual Savings Accounts
gov-isa-lisa.excerpt: You can only put <mark>£4,000 into a Lifetime ISA</mark> in a tax year, and it <mark>counts towards your £20,000</mark> allowance.

gov-isa-reset.name: GOV.UK: Individual Savings Accounts
gov-isa-reset.excerpt: Your allowance is for one tax year. <mark>You cannot carry unused allowance over</mark> to the next year.

title: Checking your credit score
question: I want to build a good credit score before I graduate. How often should I check it?
recommendation: Avoid checking your credit score more than once a year, because every check lowers it.
errorNote: Claim 2 is wrong. Checking your own credit report or score is a soft search, so it doesn't affect your score. Checking regularly is actually recommended.
parts: So look at it once a year at most, and focus on paying bills on time.

claims.text: Paying bills and credit on time is one of the main ways to build a good credit history.
Every time you check your own credit score, it leaves a mark on your file that lowers your score.

exp-cs-build.name: Experian: How to improve your credit score
exp-cs-build.excerpt: <mark>Paying on time</mark> is one of the most important things you can do to <mark>build a good credit history</mark>.

exp-cs-check.excerpt: Checking your own credit report or score is a soft search. It <mark>won't affect your credit score</mark>, so you can <mark>check it as often as you like</mark>.

title: Tax on a part-time job
question: I earn about £9,000 a year from my part-time job, but my payslip shows income tax taken off. Can I get it back?
recommendation: Yes. You probably shouldn't be paying income tax, so check your tax code and claim the money back.
errorNote: The advice is sound and every claim matches its source.
parts: You may well be owed money.

claims.text: Most people can earn £12,570 a year before paying any income tax. This is the Personal Allowance.
If you're on the wrong tax code, for example an emergency code when you start a job, you can end up paying too much.
If you've overpaid, you can claim a refund from HMRC.

gov-pa.excerpt: The standard <mark>Personal Allowance is £12,570</mark>, which is the amount of income you <mark>do not have to pay tax on</mark>.

gov-code.excerpt: You may be put on an <mark>emergency tax code</mark> when you start a new job. You could <mark>pay too much tax</mark> until your code is corrected.

title: Council tax in a student house
question: I live in a shared house with three other full-time students. Do we have to pay council tax?
recommendation: No. A house where everyone is a full-time student doesn't pay council tax, but you'll need to apply for the exemption.
errorNote: The advice is sound and every claim matches its source.

claims.text: If everyone living in a property is a full-time student, the home is exempt from council tax.
You usually need to apply to your local council, often with a certificate from your university.
